Statistical analysis was performed in GraphPad Prism 8 for Windows (v8.0.2 (263)) using unpaired two-tailed t-tests with Welch’s correction or two-way ANOVA with Sidak’s multiple comparisons, as indicated in the figure legends. Full test statistics, including exact P values, are reported in Supplementary Information Sections S2 and Section S7.

Volumetric 3D Printing. Tomographic volumetric prints were produced on a Tomolite v2.0 (Readily3D, 405 nm source; nominal voxel pitch 25 µm) with projection and continuous rotation controlled in Apparite 1.2.4. CAD files and nominal dimensions for all resolution-test geometries are provided in Section S3 of the Supplementary Information. In Apparite, the refractive index was set to 1.450—chosen to match the dominant solvent (chloroform) and consistent with related fluorinated monomers (e.g., poly(trifluoroethyl methacrylate, n ≈ 1.44). The absorption setting was 2.00 cm⁻¹, which corresponds to a base-10 absorbance of ~0.87 cm⁻¹ (conversion A = μ/ln 10); this matches the measured UV–Vis absorbance of ~0.85–0.87 cm⁻¹ for the final formulation. “Bulk Length” and “Bulk Strength” were set to Off. The vial profile was measured in situ (glass type BK7, outer diameter 7.49 mm, wall thickness 0.92 mm). After printing, parts were rinsed with acetone to remove uncured resin and post-cured under UVA (365 nm, 5 mW cm⁻², 2 h), then air-dried.

Cell culture and live dead assay. Human foreskin fibroblasts (HFF; ATCC SCRC-1041, passage 4) were cultured in high-glucose DMEM (Merck, D6429) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Sigma Aldrich, F7524) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Thermo Fisher, 15140122) at 37 °C and 5% CO₂. For direct-contact assays, cells were seeded in 96-well tissue culture plates (Thermo Fisher, 167008) at 10,000 cells/cm² (3,200 cells/well in 100 µL) and allowed to adhere for 10 h before material placement. Sterile 6 mm discs of the volumetrically 3D printed HDF-X and PTFE (benchmark) were prepared by 2 × 12 h ethanol sterilization, washed three times in DPBS, and pre-wetted in complete medium for 6 h prior to use. Discs were gently placed centrally on fibroblast monolayers using sterile forceps, while uncovered wells served as cell controls (CTRL). Cell viability was assessed at 1, 3, and 7 days post-seeding. Calcein-AM (Thermo Fisher, 65-0853-78) and propidium iodide (Thermo Fisher, P3566) were diluted to 2 µL/mL each in Fluorobrite DMEM (Thermo Fisher, A1896701). Wells were washed with DPBS, incubated with 100 µL of staining solution for 15 min at room temperature in the dark, and imaged using a Zeiss confocal microscope controlled with ZEISS ZEN Imaging Software. Images were processed in Fiji (ImageJ, v1.54) under identical exposure conditions across groups. For each condition and timepoint, three independent experiments were performed (n = 3). Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical significance was determined using two-way ANOVA with post hoc tests, with p-values indicated as ***p < 0.001 and ****p < 0.0001.

Reproducibility. Key quantitative experiments were independently replicated as indicated for each assay.

Sample size determination. No prospective power analysis was performed. Sample sizes were selected a priori based on standard practice for screening assays and materials characterization, as well as practical experimental throughput.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript focuses on a closed-loop strategy integrating volumetric 3D printing with chemical recycling for fluoropolymers. Selective urethane hydrolysis under alkaline conditions then affords 77% fluorinated monomer recovery. The application of high-concentration alkali reduces the practical application value of this work. Although this work focuses on the recycling of fluorinated materials, it essentially relies on the dissociation of urethane bonds by high-concentration alkali, and the process is cumbersome. However, there are many questions and a more detailed description is lacking in this manuscript. See the following for details:
1. In HDF-ENE synthesis, the reaction of allyl isocyanate with HDF-OH is used to form a urethane bond. Similar reactions have been presented in a number of papers and the authors are required to elaborate on this approach and the advantages of this material.
2. The generality of this work is insufficient: the recycling process was only demonstrated for one specific fluorinated material, HDF-OH, rendering the conclusions less generalizable.
3. The explanation for the latency period in photorheology needs to be verified by experiments and requires deeper interpretation.
4. The chemical recovery section mentions the condition “5 M NaOH/85 °C/2 h” without stating the basis or showing data on the effect of different base concentrations or temperatures on the recovery. Additional experimental results are recommended to illustrate the process of optimizing the conditions.
5. Printing microfluidic devices (Figure 3b) requires biocompatibility, but the cytotoxicity of HDF-X was not mentioned. Please add cytotoxicity testing. There are no in vivo or in vitro experimental results.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript reports a strategy to enable 3D printing of a fluoropolymer material using radical thiol-ene photochemistry. Importantly, the authors go on to show that these materials can be deconstructed into their constituent monomer pre-cursors, which is an important goal with respect to recovery of these environmentally harmful molecules. This contribution focuses on the use of volumetric 3D printing. This method can overcome some of the challenges that other printing methods entail such as layer-to-layer adhesion. The chemistry applied in this study does not deviate greatly from that of many printing resins, relying on creating an allyl end capped fluorinated monomer that is subsequently crosslinked with a multi arm thiol. The study is thoroughly conducted and there are some nice innovations such as the removal of inhibitors which present an advantage to the methods reported. The print resolution is impressive and the recycling studies are great to see. There are however a few amendments to the paper that should be considered prior to publication:
1) It is important to compare the materials' properties to existing fluoropolymer materials, both printed and molded so the significance of this contribution can be properly assessed.
2) I would disagree that the term 'closed loop' is appropriate to describe these materials, the fluorinated alcohol can be recovered but all other components will need to be added to a new resin to create a printable formulation and hence ca. 45% of the original chemicals are recovered to be reused and a large volume of additional chemicals is required to be added.
3) In figure 4, why is the 475 peak absent in the recycled HDF-OH?
4) Additionally, a yield of 77% of the fluorinated monomer is also not ideal as the remainder will be lost - have the authors optimized this process?

### Reviewer 3

The authors report the synthesis of an alkene-functional fluorinated monomer for thiol–ene crosslinking and its use for volumetric 3D printing. While the introduction of fluoropolymer for tomographic volumetric 3D printing has never been attempted, from my opinion, this is not sufficient in term of novelty to be considered for publication in a journal such as Nature Communications. Indeed, since the emergence of volumetric additive manufacturing (VAM), most of the photoresists developed for SLA/DLP printers have been successfully transferred to volumetric 3D printer (Bernal et al. Nature Review Materials 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-025-00785-3, The road ahead in materials and technologies for volumetric 3D printing). The challenge, if any, to successfully 3D print fluorinated monomer regarding the condition of VAM photopolymerization is not clearly discussed.
However, the authors also introduced a cleavable urethane linkage in the non degradable fluorinated precursor, allowing chemical recycling of the fluorinated monomer. This aspect is scarcely addressed for 3D printed fluoropolymer and consequently deserved to be highlighted.
Finally, some of the conclusions that the authors draw from the data appear in their current form overstated. For instance, can we really say “closed-loop volumetric 3D printing” when more than half of the chemical should be replaced to make a new print? Besides, some aspects request additional experiments or explanation to obtain a comprehensive manuscript. In its current form the manuscript appears therefore too premature for publication in Nature communications.
Please check out my comments below.
1/ Evidence of the influence of PEG1M.
Firstly, the authors have mentioned the role of PEG1M to suppress the sedimentation during printing, but no experimental evidence is given to illustrate this drawback and to explain how the authors have selected the optimal concentration (movie showing the sedimentation for different concentrations of PEG1M). See for instance SI Movie 1 & 2 of Loterie, D., Delrot, P. & Moser, C. High-resolution tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing. Nat Commun 11, 852 (2020). https://doi-org.inc.bib.cnrs.fr/10.1038/s41467-020-14630-4). Besides, the viscosity of the photoresists should be determined for concentrations of PEG1M ranging from 0 to 1.25 w% since it is a key parameter in the optimization step. The scheme depicted in Figure 2d is not sufficient to support the statement made by the authors.
Secondly, the built-in inhibition is partially attributed by the authors to the presence of PEG1M, in particularly due to the modification of the viscosity. To confirm this hypothesis, photorheology experiment has to be performed in absence of PEG1M.
2/ Origin of the delayed gelation
Beyond viscosity issue (see previous point), another hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the intrinsic inhibition of the photoresist without adding radical scavenger (such as TEMPO) is the fact that thiol-ene polymerization occurs through a step-growth mechanism. However, in their previous work with different precursors (Adv. Mater. 2023, 35 (19), e2210136. DOI: 10.1002/adma.202210136), step-growth thiol-ene polymerization was involved and the use of TEMPO was requested. I do not understand why in this specific case, step-growth will lead to delayed gelation (difference in the viscosity, photoreactivity of fluoropolymer vs its hydrogen-based counterpart?).
3/ Determination of the optimal printing dose for volumetric
Photorheological experiments are used to determine the optimal printing dose. However, the comparison between the light intensities used during photorheology experiments and those used in volumetric printing is not clearly established. This information is crucial, as photoreactivity and polymerization kinetics can be strongly influenced by light intensity and exposure time (or here manufacturing time). Moreover, experimental configuration should also influence the results: while in photorheology, the thickness is set to few hundred micrometers with continuous irradiation, for volumetric printing, the length is around 7 mm.
Clarification on this point is necessary in order to assess the transposability of results between the two experimental contexts. And light intensity and manufacturing time should be specified, the latter being also important to assess if sedimentation can occur in this time scale.
4/ Optical properties of the photoresists
The authors indicate that the absorbance value of 0.85 was chosen because, according to the Beer-Lambert law, it corresponds to a light intensity drop of about 20%. However, it is not explained why this 20% loss is considered acceptable. This threshold appears to have been set arbitrarily, without experimental or theoretical justification. It is important to explain the criteria on which this limit was based, and how it aligns with the requirements of the printing process.
Furthermore, the Tomolite printer is supposed to incorporate an optical compensation function. In the section regarding fabrication parameters, an absorption value of 2.00 cm-1 is indicated. This choice is not sufficiently explained: why was this specific value selected? In addition, the relationship between this absorption value (2.00 cm-1) and the absorbance of 0.85 is not clearly established. The correspondence between these two quantities is neither detailed nor referenced, which leads to confusion in data interpretation. A clarification on this point would be welcome.
Another aspect concerns the refractive index (1.45). It should be indicated how it has been determined and for which wavelength ?
5/ Resolution issue – feature size
The authors report feature sizes down to 15.5 µm (negative one) as the “smallest negative features reported to date for volumetric 3D printing” and highlight this fact in the abstract. How the authors can explained such resolution? Is it due to the chemistry (and why)? Or is it due to the optical system? Can they give details about the optical configuration of their printer?
According to the current experimental data, this statement is overexaggerated. The provided optical microscopic images do not allow reliable conclusions to be drawn regarding the resolution achieved. It is difficult to determine whether this is due to an actual resolution limitation, a fabrication artefact, or surface defects. It is recommended to acquire higher-quality images, particularly using a scanning electron microscope (SEM), in order to confirm the observations. CAD model should be provided to discuss printing fidelity and state on the merit of the chemistry or optical set-up.
The choice of the « Klein bottle » object for evaluating resolution appears to be poorly suited. It would be preferable to use a standardized test object, such as a grid pattern or regularly spaced lines, to allow a more rigorous and objective assessment of resolution performance. More interesting/convincing will be the printing of the microfluidic chip with internal channel of 15.5 µm width and few millimetres length (see Gong et al. Lab Chip, 2017, 17, 2899, DOI: 10.1039/c7lc00644f, Custom 3D printer and resin for 18 μm × 20 μm microfluidic flow channels)
6/ Printing fidelity
In a general manner, the CAD models should be provided with the expected dimension to assess the printing fidelity. For instance, in Figure 3b, the microfluidic system seems to be distorted (inhomogeneous geometry). Is this an expected phenomenon or a fabrication defect? Printing fidelity to be discussed.
7/ Chemical recycling
The study does not evaluate the effect of multiple recycling cycles on monomer purity, side product accumulation, or long-term property retention. Only one recycling/reprint cycle is rigorously characterized. The environmental benefit of the closed-loop system is asserted 77% monomer recovery (vs. theoretical maximum) implies significant loss after multiple recycling.
Thus, life cycle assessment may be required.
Since degradability is design-dependent owing to diffusion issue, could you indicate the shape and dimension of the volumetric printed object for such test?
What are the shape / dimension of the printed object used for the mechanical test (before and after recycling)?

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

Response to the reviewer comment:
Thank you for asking us to elaborate on the HDF-ENE design and the choice of the allyl-isocyanate urethane coupling. The functionalization route is intentional rather than novel. Using a mono- functional isocyanate avoids any chain extension during end-group installation, which can occur with diisocyanate/diol couplings. Moreover, installing allyl groups enables thiol–ene crosslinking, which follows a step-growth polymerization that is oxygen-tolerant, exhibits lower shrinkage stress, and forms more homogeneous networks with significantly increased toughness (due to the combined effect of increased crystallinity, higher ultimate strength, and larger elongation at break) relative to more commonly used (meth)acrylates. Embedding alkenes via a urethane- forming reaction also provides an alkaline-cleavable handle that releases the initial fluorinated diol, which forms the basis for the recovery of the fluorinated content of the network, as you noted in your general assessment of our work. Rather than providing a novel functionalization route, our claim of novelty lies in the integration of the reported thiol-ene fluoronetwork into volumetric printing and in closed-loop chemical recycling of its fluorinated content at very high yield (i.e., 97.4%).
However, in order to provide insight to the reader related to our choice of functionalization and the unique attributes of our developed material, we have introduced the following paragraph in the synthesis section of the main article:
“Allyl isocyanate end-capping was used because it is robust, operates under mild conditions, and scales well. The reaction selectively functionalizes terminal diols while avoiding the chain extension common to diisocyanate/diol couplings.26 Finally, the introduced alkene end groups enable step-growth thiol–ene crosslinking that is oxygen-tolerant, yields uniform and low-shrinkage networks with improved toughness compared to more conventional (meth)acrylate crosslinking (vide infra).”

Response to the reviewer comment:
Thank you for foregrounding generality. The study was designed as an integrated proof-of-concept that follows one system through the full arc of material development → tomographic volumetric printing → chemical recycling → re-functionalization → re-use. Prompted by your comment, we have made the scope explicit and reframed the paper as a single, carefully documented exemplar rather than a broad survey across different fluorinated polymers. Extending the workflow to additional fluoropolymers would require de novo optimization of solubility and work-up, optical attenuation and dose windows, resin rheology, and alkaline depolymerization for each precursor; those are substantive, independent efforts that fall beyond the scope of the present study. We therefore chose depth over breadth and tightened the claims accordingly, while emphasizing the aspects that are transferable (workflow, analysis, and documentation).
Concretely, we narrowed the language throughout the article so readers see at a glance what is— and is not—being claimed.
The title now reflects the singular exemplar “Volumetric 3D Printing of a Fluoropolymer and Closed-Loop Chemical Recycling of its Fluorinated Content.”
The abstract’s final sentence has been revised to: “This represents the first demonstration of high- resolution tomographic volumetric printing of a fluoropolymer with closed-loop chemical recycling of its fluorinated content.”
In the introduction has been revised to: “While we report a single-system exemplar which we follow through tomographic volumetric 3D printing, fluorinated monomer recycling, refunctionalization, and reuse, the reported workflow is modular and can be adapted by others to different fluorinated precursors.”

3. The explanation for the latency period in photorheology needs to be verified by experiments and requires deeper interpretation.
Response to the reviewer comment:
Thank you for pressing us to verify the origin of the photorheological latency—this was an important check. We repeated the measurements on matched formulations with and without PEG1M under identical conditions. Interestingly, the latency period and the transient dip in G′ were essentially unchanged, which does not support a PEG1M-driven viscosity origin. We therefore withdraw that explanation in the main text and now attribute the delay primarily to step- growth gelation in the bifunctional-ene/multifunctional-thiol network: gelation—and thus the rise in G′—is expected only at comparatively high functional conversion (consistent with Flory– Stockmayer considerations for tetrafunctional thiol with bifunctional ene). A small initial decrease in G′ is plausibly due to the exothermicity of the reaction. We note, however, that formulation-specific factors (solvation of the fluorinated backbone, oxygen solubility, solvent environment and local microstructure, and light intensity/exposure history) can modulate latency even in oxygen-tolerant thiol–ene systems. Fully disentangling these influences is beyond the scope here; we present step-growth gelation as the leading explanation and document the control data so readers can judge the assignment, but prompt readers to approach the current hypothesis with caution.
We have incorporated these new experiments and insights into the main article as follows:
“Two hypotheses were considered for the rheological latency: (i) a PEG1M-induced viscosity barrier that delays network formation, and (ii) the intrinsic gelation threshold of step-growth thiol–ene networks. Matched photorheology on formulations with and without PEG1M yielded the same latency period, excluding hypothesis (i) (Section S1.4). We therefore attribute the latency primarily to hypothesis (ii): by Flory–Stockmayer theory, an elastically percolated network forms only beyond ~58% functional-group conversion for a tetrafunctional thiol with a bifunctional alkene.28,29 However, it should be noted that the stated hypothesis should be interpreted with caution, as the onset and magnitude of the latency can be affected by other factors (e.g., fluorinated-backbone solvation, oxygen solubility, the solvent environment, local microstructure, and light intensity-dependent kinetics). Fully disentangling these contributions lies beyond the scope of the present study. Separately, the small decrease in G′ observed immediately after illumination but prior to gelation is consistent with a modest reaction exotherm that transiently raises temperature, lowers viscosity, and increases mobility.”
Additionally, we have included the photo-rheological data in Section S1.4 of the Supporting Information as shown below:
“S1.4 Influence of PEG1M on the inhibition period in photo-rheology
To test whether the rheological latency originates from PEG1M-induced viscosity effects, we repeated photorheology on matched formulations with and without PEG1M under identical irradiation; the latency and G′ trajectory were unchanged.
Figure S6. Photorheology with/without PEG1M at 405 nm, 10 mW cm⁻²; light on at t = 10 s. Solid line: storage modulus (G′); dashed line: loss modulus (G″). Both traces show similar latency and rise, indicating PEG1M is not the origin.”
4. The chemical recovery section mentions the condition “5 M NaOH/85 °C/2 h” without stating the basis or showing data on the effect of different base concentrations or temperatures on the recovery. Additional experimental results are recommended to illustrate the process of optimizing the conditions.
Response to the reviewer comment:
The authors agree that rigor around the recycling step is essential. Because all three reviewers independently raised this point, we executed a full condition matrix and were able to increase the recovery of the fluorinated monomer to 97.4 % ± 2.1 %. Thus, 97.4% of the fluorinated monomer is recovered after the first recycle–reuse loop, and that retained fraction compounds with each additional loop. In practice, this means that about 88% remains after five cycles and about 77% remains after ten cycles.
We systematically screened NaOH concentrations of 1.0, 2.5, and 5.0 M at 85 °C across hydrolytic degradation times ranging from 0.5 to 16 h. For each condition, we executed the complete workflow—alkaline reflux depolymerization, neutralization, purification, and drying—with identical resin mass and solution volume. This investigation, initiated by the reviewers’ comments, increased the fluorinated-monomer recovery to 97.4% ± 2.1% at 2.5 M NaOH for 3 h, and is now used throughout the manuscript. Finally, repeatability at this condition was confirmed in triplicate (s.d. = 2.1%), significantly reducing cumulative loss over multiple reuse cycles.
We have included the following discussion related to the parameter screening into the main manuscript:
“After establishing a general workflow—alkaline reflux depolymerization, neutralization, purification, and drying— through which the fluorinated diol could be recovered from volumetrically 3D printed constructs, the degradation conditions were optimized to maximize the chemical recycling yield of the fluorinated diol (Section S5). More precisely, a condition screen at 85 °C was performed across NaOH concentrations of 1.0, 2.5, and 5.0 M and depolymerization times from 0.5–16 h, executing the complete sequence for every timepoint. The optimal condition (2.5 M NaOH for 3 h) afforded a recovery of 97.4 % ± 2.1 % (n = 3). At this per-cycle recovery, the theoretical retained fraction after ten recycle–reuse cycles is ≈76.8 % of the original fluorinated content (see Supporting Information, Section S5, for the full data and calculations).
The recovery–time profiles delineate two regimes, depicted in Figure S10. In the kinetic regime, yield increases to a concentration-dependent maximum that is reached earlier at higher [NaOH] (5 M: ~1–1.5 h; 2.5 M: ~3 h; 1 M: no maximum within 16 h). This trend is consistent with base-catalyzed urethane cleavage in which the apparent rate scales with hydroxide activity (pseudo-first-order, 𝑘 ≈ 𝑘 [𝑂𝐻−]). Beyond the maximum, the 𝑜𝑏𝑠 𝑏 isolated yield declines at 2.5–5 M and approaches a plateau. It is hypothesized that the gradual formation of crosslinked/aggregated side-product particulates during prolonged alkaline treatment physically entrap a fraction of the fluorinated diol and resist subsequent extraction. Once the population of such particulates saturates, the recovery approaches the observed plateau. The optimum at 2.5 M, 3 h therefore marks the intersection of fast cleavage kinetics with minimal secondary entrainment, resulting in a recycling yield of the fluorinated monomer of 97.4 % ± 2.1 % (n = 3).”

“Chemical recycling of HDF-OH from HDF-X. Prior to alkaline cleavage, volumetrically printed constructs were briefly ground with a mortar and pestle to eliminate geometry- dependent effects during degradation. A condition screen was performed at 85 °C under reflux, varying [NaOH] to 1.0, 2.5, and 5.0 M, and reaction time (0.5–16 h). For each condition, the same resin mass and solution volume were used and the full workflow was executed—alkaline depolymerization → neutralization to pH ≈ 7 with 1 M HCl → solvent removal by rotary evaporation → dissolution of the residue in diethyl ether (Et₂O) → filtration of insolubles → solvent removal → drying—to isolate HDF-OH (see Supporting Information Section S5). The optimized condition was identified as 2.5 M NaOH for 3 h at 85 °C, which afforded 97.4 % ± 2.1 % recovery (n = 3). For a representative batch, ground material (300 mg) was charged to a 50 mL round-bottom flask with 10 mL of 2.5 M NaOH and heated at 85 °C under reflux for 3 h. The reaction mixture was then neutralized to pH ≈ 7 by gradual addition of 1 M HCl. After neutralization, acetone was added to the aqueous phase (1:1 v/v water:acetone) to facilitate co-evaporation and streamline water removal during rotary evaporation. The mixture was concentrated by rotary evaporation to remove water and acetone, affording a solid residue. The residue was dissolved in diethyl ether (Et₂O), and the mixture was filtered to remove insoluble inorganic and polymeric by-products. The Et₂O-soluble fraction was collected, while the retained solids were washed thoroughly with deionized water to remove NaCl and other inorganic residues, then rinsed with hexane to displace residual water. The washed solids were subsequently re- extracted with Et₂O to recover any remaining HDF-OH. The combined Et₂O extracts were concentrated by rotary evaporation, and the resulting product was dried under vacuum at 40 °C for 2 h to afford purified HDF-OH, which was then re-functionalized as described in the preceding section.”

6. The authors should include a supplementary table comparing resolution metrics of volumetric 3D printing technologies, explicitly demonstrating that their 15.5 μm negative feature size represents the smallest reported to date.
Response to the reviewer comment:
Thank you for recommending a comparative resolution summary. Given that both you and Reviewer 3 raised concerns about our earlier single-value emphasis, we have revised the way we report feature size throughout the article. Rather than highlighting one minimum, we now report condition-bound feature sizes with explicit CAD linkage across several demanding geometries, while keeping the central contribution—volumetric 3D printing of a fluorinated network together with closed-loop chemical recycling of the fluorinated content—front and center.
In tomographic volumetric printing, the smallest reliably formed feature is not dictated by optics alone. It reflects the design-dependent computational contrast in back-projection, resin kinetics around gelation, viscosity with associated diffusion and sedimentation during and after exposure, polymerization shrinkage, and post-processing choices such as wash solvent and time. Because these factors couple, assigning a particular small feature to a single cause would be speculative and lies beyond the scope of the present work. Rather than advancing an ultimate resolution limit, we document what is reproducibly achieved under clearly specified conditions and provide the information needed for others to interpret those outcomes.
To position the results, the Supporting Information now includes a curated overview of reported feature sizes in tomographic volumetric printing derived from a screen of 37 studies; fourteen papers that list explicit numerical values were retained. Table S1 collates those minima to indicate what has been achieved in the field and to contextualize the condition-bound features reported here. Many publications present a single “best-case” feature size without linking back to design. In tomographic volumetric 3D printing, such single-feature reporting is not adequate due to its relatively low computational contrast (i.e., the difference between the light dose that in-part and out-of-part voxels receive), as compared to stereolithography (SLA) or digital light processing (DLP), where out-of-part voxels typically don’t receive any light (i.e., perfect computational contrast). As a result, the out-of-part voxels fundamentally limit the dose that in-part voxels can receive, and, as a result, the apparent feature size can depend strongly on the washing step. In the revised manuscript, we make this linkage explicit.
We also strengthened the experimental evidence underlying our values. The single-geometry showcase has been replaced by a multi-geometry presentation. For each design, we report the measured feature size alongside the corresponding CAD dimension at that exact location, so any deviation is explicit. The images show continuous features rather than surface artefacts, and the CAD files with nominal dimensions are provided so readers can assess fidelity directly. Firstly, related to the aforementioned discussion, the following text has been added to the Supporting Information:
“S3. Feature-size in tomographic volumetric 3D printing. In tomographic volumetric printing, the smallest reliably formed feature is not dictated by optics alone. It is governed by the design-dependent computational contrast in back-projection, resin kinetics around gelation, viscosity together with diffusion and sedimentation during and after exposure, polymerization shrinkage, and post-processing choices such as wash solvent and time. Rather than advancing an ultimate resolution limit, we document what is reproducibly achieved under fixed conditions and provide the information needed for others to interpret those outcomes.
S3.1 Literature positioning of volumetric 3D printing resolution. To contextualize the obtained feature sizes in the current work, we screened 37 publications on tomographic volumetric 3D printing and retained 14 that report explicit numerical values (restricted to tomographic volumetric 3D printing and excluding post-sintered ceramics). Table S1 collates these reported minima. Only two papers provide a direct design-to- measurement comparison: Kelly et al. (2019) report a 200 µm tail-fin tip radius versus a 400 µm design (sharper than intended), and Orth et al. (2023) report 195–200 µm versus ~180 µm for a gyroid wall and 580 µm versus ~500 µm for a pore. Most articles list single ‘best-case’ values with little to no linkage to CAD or reproducibility. The purpose of Table S1 is transparency: to position achievable feature sizes in tomographic volumetric printing and to provide readers with context for interpreting the condition-bound feature sizes reported here.
S3.2 Experimental and theoretical feature sizes of volumetric 3D printed constructs. Figure S8 pairs each CAD model with its simulated back-projection contrast and a micrograph at the narrowest measured element. Across the four designs shown, the smallest observed features are ~56 µm, ~66 µm, ~97 µm, and ~254 µm; the corresponding CAD dimensions at those exact locations are indicated in the contrast panels. Set against the survey in Table S1, these values sit among the smallest polymer features reported for tomographic volumetric printing. Only a few studies approach this scale with comparable clarity of reporting; notably, Toombs et al. (2022) demonstrate ~20 µm polymer features on a different platform. It should be noted that the very small ‘positive’ values reported by Bernal et al. (2022) and by Falandt et al. (2023) correspond to the outermost tip of a star-shaped element; such apex measurements are highly sensitive to washing and do not represent generally reproducible line or strut widths.
The gap between CAD and experiment is expected. In tomographic exposure, the achievable width at a given location is governed by local computational contrast from back-projection, the resin’s conversion profile near gelation, and the subsequent washing step, which can remove weakly crosslinked material at feature edges. Additional contributors include polymerization shrinkage and any swelling or surface relaxation during post-processing. Because most papers in the field report single ‘best-case’ numbers without CAD-to-measurement linkage—Kelly et al. (2019) and Orth et al. (2023) are rare exceptions—Figure S8 provides that linkage explicitly so that readers can interpret the condition-bound features observed here.

Importantly, the authors go on to show that these materials can be deconstructed into their constituent monomer pre-cursors, which is an important goal with respect to recovery of these environmentally harmful molecules. This contribution focuses on the use of volumetric 3D printing. This method can overcome some of the challenges that other printing methods entail such as layer-to-layer adhesion. The chemistry applied in this study does not deviate greatly from that of many printing resins, relying on creating an allyl end capped fluorinated monomer that is subsequently crosslinked with a multi arm thiol. The study is thoroughly conducted and there are some nice innovations such as the removal of inhibitors which present an advantage to the methods reported. The print resolution is impressive and the recycling studies are great to see. There are however a few amendments to the paper that should be considered prior to publication:
1. It is important to compare the materials' properties to existing fluoropolymer materials, both printed and molded so the significance of this contribution can be properly assessed.
Response to the reviewer comment:
Thank you for asking for a benchmark—this was an important gap in our initial submission, as we had mainly focused on showing property retention before and after chemical recycling. Your point helped us reframe the contribution in terms of where the material sits among established, gold- standard fluoropolymers. We have now benchmarked our material against a gold-standard fluoropolymer (molded, high–molar-mass PTFE).
The developed system is a crosslinkable, semi-crystalline fluorinated thermoset that operates above T at room temperature. Under tension, it shows a broad elastic window and large post- g yield ductility, yielding a work-to-break of 22.3 ± 13.2 J cm⁻³ versus 21.6 ± 10.4 J cm⁻³ for PTFE— statistically indistinguishable under our test geometry. In other words, our crosslinked network matches the toughness of PTFE, a high molar mass thermoplastic which is used across a wide range of applications. We attribute this toughness to a synergy between crystallinity coupled with a homogeneous thiol–ene network topology.
Regarding ‘printed vs molded,’ because light-based 3D-printable fluorinated resins are not commercially available, and extrusion introduces process-dependent microstructures, we opted for a material benchmark to enable a fair comparison by class (i.e., thermoplastic vs thermoset).
Related to the benchmark, we have included the following discussion in the main manuscript
“To contextualize performance against the fluoropolymer state-of-the-art, we benchmarked the material against a food-grade PTFE reference (also known by the brand name Teflon). PTFE shows the expected semicrystalline thermoplastic signature with higher stiffness and ultimate strength (Young’s modulus 458.6 ± 0.1 MPa; ultimate tensile strength 27.0 ± 0.3 MPa) but a lower elongation at break (188 ± 5 %). The developed semi- crystalline fluorinated network operates above its glass transition (≈1.3 °C) and retains residual crystallinity (crystallization and melting at ≈55 °C and ≈64 °C), which—together with a homogeneous thiol–ene network topology—yields large post-yield deformation, and a very high elongation at break (409 ± 108 %). Despite a lower stiffness and ultimate tensile strength (Young’s modulus 32.3 ± 14 MPa; ultimate tensile strength 6.6 ± 1.8 MPa), the extensive ductility gives a comparable toughness (work-to-break) under our test geometry. The resulting toughness is 22.3 ± 13.2 J cm⁻³ for HDF-X and 21.6 ± 10.4 J cm⁻³ for PTFE, i.e., comparable toughness within experimental variance. In other words, our crosslinked network matches the toughness of PTFE, a high molar mass thermoplastic which is used across a wide range of applications. Thermogravimetric analysis at 2% mass loss places the degradation onset near 295 °C for the network and 547 ± 0.4 °C for PTFE; while PTFE retains the higher thermal margin, the network’s stability is sufficient for many service environments well below 300 °C. Full datasets, replicate statistics, and analysis procedures are provided in Supporting Information §7.”

Response to the reviewer comment:
Thank you for the careful point on terminology. We agree that “closed loop” should be used with a clear system boundary. In our work, the loop is closed for the fluorinated content: alkaline urethane cleavage releases HDF-OH, which is re-functionalized and re-used; the non-fluorinated auxiliaries are replenished each cycle. To remove any ambiguity, we have made this explicit throughout the article and revised its title to: “Volumetric 3D Printing of a Fluoropolymer and Closed-Loop Chemical Recycling of its Fluorinated Content.” This wording makes clear that the closed loop pertains to the fluorinated fraction of the network.
The reviewer is also right that, in the current formulation, approximately 52 wt.% of the network is fluorinated content; the remainder must be replenished upon reprinting. Per cycle, however, the fluorinated monomer is recovered at 97.4% ± 2.1%, and we report the corresponding multi- cycle retention in the manuscript and the Supporting Information (refer to our reply to your 4th comment). Importantly, the recyclable fraction can be increased by raising the molar mass of the fluorinated diol, which directly increases the weight fraction of fluorinated content in the network. We therefore added a short analysis showing how the overall recyclable fraction increases to 82, 90, 93, and 94%, when the diol molar mass is increased to 2 000, 4 000, 6 000, and 8 000 g mol⁻¹, respectively (calculations and assumptions are provided below).
We chose, however, not to broaden the present study to multiple fluoropolymer backbones with different molar masses because our aim here is an integrated and detailed proof-of-concept that runs the full arc: material development → volumetric printing → chemical recycling → refunctionalization → reuse. Extending to additional precursors would require de novo optimization of the synthesis and workup, volumetric 3D printing, depolymerization parameters as well as purification, and full characterization—which was considered beyond the scope of the current contribution.

3. In figure 4, why is the 475 peak absent in the recycled HDF-OH?
Response to the reviewer comment:
Thank you for asking us to clarify the LC–MS assignments. For HDE-OH (neutral exact mass 462.1305), the peak at 461 corresponds to the deprotonated ion [M–H]⁻ (calc. 461.1227). The signals at 507 and 521 are common anion-adducts formed in negative-mode ESI from trace mobile-phase acids: [M+HCOO]⁻ (formate; calc. 507.1282) and [M+CH₃COO]⁻ (acetate; calc. 521.1438); 522 is the M+1 isotope of the acetate adduct.
However, the ∼475 signal does not seem to match any obvious adduct of HDE-OH. Yet, the functionalized material was recrystallized, and after recycling, it is therefore much purer than the pristine commercial sample; at LC–MS sensitivity, the 475 feature is consistent with a trace side component present only in the pristine lot. Our working hypothesis is a trifluoroacetate adduct of a lower-mass homolog (e.g., HDF-OH, neutral 362.1148): [homolog + CF₃COO – H]⁻ calc. 475.0999 m/z. Recrystallization is assumed to remove this minor homolog, resulting in the absence of the 475 peak in the recycled HDE-OH.
4. Additionally, a yield of 77% of the fluorinated monomer is also not ideal as the remainder will be lost - have the authors optimized this process?
Response to the reviewer comment:
The authors agree that rigor around the recycling step is essential. Because all three reviewers independently raised this point, we executed a full condition matrix and were able to increase the recovery of the fluorinated monomer to 97.4 % ± 2.1 %. Thus, 97.4% of the fluorinated monomer is recovered after the first recycle–reuse loop, and that retained fraction compounds with each additional loop. In practice, this means that about 88% remains after five cycles and about 77% remains after ten cycles.
We systematically screened NaOH concentrations of 1.0, 2.5, and 5.0 M at 85 °C across hydrolytic degradation times ranging from 0.5 to 16 h. For each condition, we executed the complete workflow—alkaline reflux depolymerization, liquid–liquid extraction, aqueous washing/neutralization, and drying— with identical resin mass and solution volume. This investigation, initiated by the reviewers’ comments, increased the fluorinated-monomer recovery to 97.4% ± 2.1% at 2.5 M NaOH for 3 h, and is now used throughout the manuscript. Finally, repeatability at this condition was confirmed in triplicate (s.d. = 2.1%), significantly reducing cumulative loss over multiple reuse cycles.
We have included the following discussion related to the parameter screening into the main manuscript:
“After establishing a general workflow—alkaline reflux depolymerization, neutralization, purification, and drying— through which the fluorinated diol could be recovered from volumetrically 3D printed constructs, the degradation conditions were optimized to maximize the chemical recycling yield of the fluorinated diol (Section S5). More precisely, a condition screen at 85 °C was performed across NaOH concentrations of 1.0, 2.5, and 5.0 M and depolymerization times from 0.5–16 h, executing the complete sequence for every timepoint. The optimal condition (2.5 M NaOH for 3 h) afforded a recovery of 97.4 % ± 2.1 % (n = 3). At this per-cycle recovery, the theoretical retained fraction after ten recycle–reuse cycles is ≈76.8 % of the original fluorinated content (see Supporting Information, Section S5, for the full data and calculations).
The recovery–time profiles delineate two regimes, depicted in Figure S10. In the kinetic regime, yield increases to a concentration-dependent maximum that is reached earlier at higher [NaOH] (5 M: ~1–1.5 h; 2.5 M: ~3 h; 1 M: no maximum within 16 h). This trend is consistent with base-catalyzed urethane cleavage in which the apparent rate scales with hydroxide activity (pseudo-first-order, 𝑘 ≈ 𝑘 [𝑂𝐻−]). Beyond the maximum, the 𝑜𝑏𝑠 𝑏 isolated yield declines at 2.5–5 M and approaches a plateau. It is hypothesized that the gradual formation of crosslinked/aggregated side-product particulates during prolonged alkaline treatment physically entrap a fraction of the fluorinated diol and resist subsequent extraction. Once the population of such particulates saturates, the recovery approaches the observed plateau. The optimum at 2.5 M, 3 h therefore marks the intersection of fast cleavage kinetics with minimal secondary entrainment, resulting in a recycling yield of the fluorinated monomer of 97.4 % ± 2.1 % (n = 3).”

“Chemical recycling of HDF-OH from HDF-X. Prior to alkaline cleavage, volumetrically printed constructs were briefly ground with a mortar and pestle to eliminate geometry- dependent effects during degradation. A condition screen was performed at 85 °C under reflux, varying [NaOH] to 1.0, 2.5, and 5.0 M, and reaction time (0.5–16 h). For each condition, the same resin mass and solution volume were used and the full workflow was executed—alkaline depolymerization → neutralization to pH ≈ 7 with 1 M HCl → solvent removal by rotary evaporation → dissolution of the residue in diethyl ether (Et₂O) → filtration of insolubles → solvent removal → drying—to isolate HDF-OH (see Supporting Information Section S5). The optimized condition was identified as 2.5 M NaOH for 3 h at 85 °C, which afforded 97.4 % ± 2.1 % recovery (n = 3). For a representative batch, ground material (300 mg) was charged to a 50 mL round-bottom flask with 10 mL of 2.5 M NaOH and heated at 85 °C under reflux for 3 h. The reaction mixture was then neutralized to pH ≈ 7 by gradual addition of 1 M HCl. After neutralization, acetone was added to the aqueous phase (1:1 v/v water:acetone) to facilitate co-evaporation and streamline water removal during rotary evaporation. The mixture was concentrated by rotary evaporation to remove water and acetone, affording a solid residue. The residue was dissolved in diethyl ether (Et₂O), and the mixture was filtered to remove insoluble inorganic and polymeric by-products. The Et₂O-soluble fraction was collected, while the retained solids were washed thoroughly with deionized water to remove NaCl and other inorganic residues, then rinsed with hexane to displace residual water. The washed solids were subsequently re- extracted with Et₂O to recover any remaining HDF-OH. The combined Et₂O extracts were concentrated by rotary evaporation, and the resulting product was dried under vacuum at 40 °C for 2 h to afford purified HDF-OH, which was then re-functionalized as described in the preceding section.”
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author)
The authors report the synthesis of an alkene-functional fluorinated monomer for thiol–ene crosslinking and its use for volumetric 3D printing. While the introduction of fluoropolymer for tomographic volumetric 3D printing has never been attempted, from my opinion, this is not sufficient in term of novelty to be considered for publication in a journal such as Nature Communications. Indeed, since the emergence of volumetric additive manufacturing (VAM), most of the photoresists developed for SLA/DLP printers have been successfully transferred to volumetric 3D printer (Bernal et al. Nature Review Materials 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-025-00785-3, The road ahead in materials and technologies for volumetric 3D printing). The challenge, if any, to successfully 3D print fluorinated monomer regarding the condition of VAM photopolymerization is not clearly discussed.
However, the authors also introduced a cleavable urethane linkage in the non degradable fluorinated precursor, allowing chemical recycling of the fluorinated monomer. This aspect is scarcely addressed for 3D printed fluoropolymer and consequently deserved to be highlighted.
Finally, some of the conclusions that the authors draw from the data appear in their current form overstated. For instance, can we really say “closed-loop volumetric 3D printing” when more than half of the chemical should be replaced to make a new print? Besides, some aspects request additional experiments or explanation to obtain a comprehensive manuscript. In its current form the manuscript appears therefore too premature for publication in Nature communications.
Please check out my comments below.
1. Evidence of the influence of PEG1M. Firstly, the authors have mentioned the role of PEG1M to suppress the sedimentation during printing, but no experimental evidence is given to illustrate this drawback and to explain how the authors have selected the optimal concentration (movie showing the sedimentation for different concentrations of PEG1M). See for instance SI Movie 1 & 2 of Loterie, D., Delrot, P. & Moser, C. High-resolution tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing. Nat Commun 11, 852 (2020). https://doi-org.inc.bib.cnrs.fr/10.1038/s41467-020-14630-4). Besides, the viscosity of the photoresists should be determined for concentrations of PEG1M ranging from 0 to 1.25 w% since it is a key parameter in the optimization step. The scheme depicted in Figure 2d is not sufficient to support the statement made by the authors.

From these videos, we have exported the timeframes at 27 seconds, which is 3 seconds after the print has finished. The respective timeframes show that only the resin containing 1.25 wt.% is able to prevent sedimentation within this time window. In addition, we included viscosity measurements for the resin without and with the optimal concentration of 1.25 wt.% PEG1M.

Response to the reviewer comment:
Thank you for pressing us to verify the origin of the photorheological latency—this was an important check. We repeated the measurements on matched formulations with and without PEG1M under identical conditions. Interestingly, the latency period and the transient dip in G′ were essentially unchanged, which does not support a PEG1M-driven viscosity origin. We therefore withdraw the earlier viscosity-based explanation and retain PEG1M only to mitigate sedimentation during printing (see Comment 1).
Our current hypothesis is that the apparent delay reflects step-growth gelation in the tetra- thiol/bis-allyl formulation: an elastically percolated network—and thus a rise in G′—is expected only after a comparatively high functional-group conversion (≈58% for an ideal 4/2 system, Flory– Stockmayer). As correctly noted by the reviewer, this conversion threshold is also present in our earlier thiol–ene work (Adv. Mater. 2023, 35, e2210136), where we added TEMPO to deliberately extend the pre-gel window. The difference in practice between the two systems likely stems from resin-specific factors: in the present resin, the bifunctional alkene has a much lower molar mass (≈462 g mol⁻¹ versus 2 000–8 000 g mol⁻¹ previously), leading to shorter strands between crosslinks and different kinetics; the fluorinated backbone also differs from poly(ε-caprolactone) in polarity and oxygen/solvation behavior; and the volumetric dose schedule and employed photo-initiator are not identical. Together, these effects plausibly shift the time required to reach percolation so that an added inhibitor is unnecessary here. We emphasize that this mechanistic assignment should be interpreted with caution; fully deconvolving backbone, oxygen partitioning, solvent environment, and local microstructure lies beyond the present scope. In the revision, we include the +/− PEG1M datasets, withdraw the viscosity hypothesis, and present step-growth gelation as the leading explanation, while highlighting that the reported hypothesis should be interpreted with caution.
We have incorporated these new insights into the main article as follows:
“Two hypotheses were considered for the rheological latency: (i) a PEG1M-induced viscosity barrier that delays network formation, and (ii) the intrinsic gelation threshold of step-growth thiol–ene networks. Matched photorheology on formulations with and without PEG1M yielded the same inhibition period, excluding hypothesis (i) (Section S1.4). We therefore attribute the latency primarily to hypothesis (ii): by Flory–Stockmayer theory, an elastically percolated network forms only beyond ~58% functional-group conversion for a tetrafunctional thiol with a bifunctional alkene.28,29 However, it should be noted that the stated hypothesis should be interpreted with caution, as the onset and magnitude of the latency can be affected by other contributions (e.g., fluorinated- backbone solvation, oxygen solubility, the solvent environment, local microstructure, and light intensity-dependent kinetics). Fully disentangling these contributions lies beyond the scope of the present study. Separately, the small decrease in G′ observed immediately after illumination but prior to gelation is consistent with a modest reaction exotherm that transiently raises temperature, lowers viscosity, and increases mobility.”
Additionally, we have included the photo-rheological data in the Supporting Information as shown below:
“S1.4 Influence of PEG1M on the inhibition period in photo-rheology
To test whether the rheological latency originates from PEG1M-induced viscosity effects, we repeated photorheology on matched formulations with and without PEG1M under identical irradiation; the latency and G′ trajectory were unchanged.
Figure S6. Photorheology with/without PEG1M at 405 nm, 10 mW cm⁻²; light on at t = 10 s. Solid line: storage modulus (G′); dashed line: loss modulus (G″). Both traces show similar latency and rise, indicating PEG1M is not the origin.”
3. Determination of the optimal printing dose for volumetric. Photorheological experiments are used to determine the optimal printing dose. However, the comparison between the light intensities used during photorheology experiments and those used in volumetric printing is not clearly established. This information is crucial, as photoreactivity and polymerization kinetics can be strongly influenced by light intensity and exposure time (or here manufacturing time). Moreover, experimental configuration should also influence the results: while in photorheology, the thickness is set to few hundred micrometers with continuous irradiation, for volumetric printing, the length is around 7 mm. Clarification on this point is necessary in order to assess the transposability of results between the two experimental contexts. And light intensity and manufacturing time should be specified, the latter being also important to assess if sedimentation can occur in this time scale.
Response to the reviewer comment:
Thank you for this careful and expert comment. You are absolutely right that light intensity and attenuation govern transposability, and our original text did not make that mapping explicit enough. In the present work, photorheology is used to define a kinetic light-dose window under conditions that match volumetric printing in wavelength and irradiance: both setups use 405 nm, and the irradiance at the sample is comparable (photorheology ≈ 9.5 mW cm⁻²; volumetric 3D printing average ≈ 9.56 mW cm⁻², measured radiometrically). The optimal rheological dose is identified by the computational contrast (i.e., the ratio of the light dose that the out-of-part voxels receive to the light dose that the in-part voxels receive) and the gelation light dose.
We do not convert this delivered rheology dose into a tomographic “absorbed dose.” Instead, the two volumetric 3D printing-specific factors that differ from rheology are handled separately: attenuation across the ~7 mm path is addressed during resin design by Beer–Lambert calculations used to set the photoinitiator concentration at 405 nm, and sedimentation is addressed by increasing viscosity with PEG1M and verifying—by time-lapse videos—that no visible settling occurs over the 24 s manufacturing time used here.
We have revised the manuscript to state explicitly the wavelength, irradiances, and manufacturing time; to clarify that photorheology yields the kinetic window while attenuation and sedimentation are treated separately. We would like to note, however, that this framework builds on prior published work where these crucial considerations are discussed in much greater depth, and, for readers interested in the full methodology that links photorheology to tomographic printing (kinetic modelling, FTIR validation on dose-stopped rheology samples, and a discussion of reciprocity and geometric limits), we have made the reference to our previously published framework more clear throughout the manuscript.
The following text was introduced to the manuscript to address the reviewer’s comment:
“To identify a suitable volumetric 3D printing light dose, photorhelogy and volumetric printing were wavelength- and irradiance-matched (405 nm in both cases; ≈ 9.5 mW cm⁻² at the rheology sample and 9.56 mW cm⁻² average in volumetric 3D printing). In combination with a computational contrast of 0.5–an appropriate computational contrast for most designs in tomographic volumetric 3D printing–dose thresholds, at which in-part voxels begin to gel while out-of-part voxels remain sub-gel, can be established. The middle of this range then corresponds to the selected light dose of 180 mJ cm⁻², at which in-part voxels are sufficiently cured to resist gravity-driven collapse while out-of-part voxels remain below the gelation threshold.22 This photorheological framework does not account for attenuation across the ~7 mm path during tomographic printing or for sedimentation, owing to the small rheometer gap (~300 µm) and static geometry. These two factors were therefore addressed separately before applying the photorheological window—attenuation by setting the photoinitiator concentration via Beer–Lambert calculations for the vial geometry (Section S1.1 and S1.2), and sedimentation by viscosity tuning with PEG1M (Section S1.3). For full methodological details underpinning this framework refer to the cited work.22”
4. Optical properties of the photoresists. The authors indicate that the absorbance value of 0.85 was chosen because, according to the Beer-Lambert law, it corresponds to a light intensity drop of about 20%. However, it is not explained why this 20% loss is considered acceptable. This threshold appears to have been set arbitrarily, without experimental or theoretical justification. It is important to explain the criteria on which this limit was based, and how it aligns with the requirements of the printing process. Furthermore, the Tomolite printer is supposed to incorporate an optical compensation function. In the section regarding fabrication parameters, an absorption value of 2.00 cm-1 is indicated. This choice is not sufficiently explained: why was this specific value selected? In addition, the relationship between this absorption value (2.00 cm-1) and the absorbance of 0.85 is not clearly established. The correspondence between these two quantities is neither detailed nor referenced, which leads to confusion in data interpretation. A clarification on this point would be welcome. Another aspect concerns the refractive index (1.45). It should be indicated how it has been determined and for which wavelength ?
Response to the reviewer comment:
Thank you for this careful observation. You are right that our wording around “~20% drop” reads as arbitrary. In practice, the attenuation setting was chosen to sit within the optical- compensation envelope of the Tomolite/Apparite reconstruction at 405 nm. The software compensates through-volume attenuation reliably up to a Napierian absorption coefficient μ = 2.0 cm⁻¹. We therefore set the initiator loading so that the resin’s attenuation is at (but not above) this limit. In base-10 terms, this corresponds to an absorbance per centimetre of A = μ/ln 10 ≈ 2.0/2.303 ≈ 0.87, which matches the A ≈ 0.85 cm⁻¹ we report by UV–Vis. Selecting this value balances photoreactivity (high photoinitiator concentration) with the attenuation compensation and is not an arbitrary “percentage loss” rule. We have revised the discussion in the main manuscript as shown below:
“To ensure accurate dose delivery during tomographic exposure, the photoinitiator concentration was determined using Beer–Lambert calculations together with the optical-compensation range of the printer software at 405 nm. The Tomolite/Apparite reconstruction compensates attenuation up to a Napierian absorption coefficient μ = 2.0 cm⁻¹; we therefore selected a resin absorbance near this upper bound. In base-10 terms this corresponds to A = μ/ln 10 ≈ 0.87 cm⁻¹, consistent with the measured UV–Vis absorbance of ≈ 0.85–0.87 cm⁻¹ for the final formulation (Section S1.1 and S1.2). This choice maximizes photoreactivity while remaining within the instrument’s compensation envelope.”
Finally, regarding the refractive index used in reconstruction, we set n = 1.45 at 405 nm. This value was chosen by reference to the dominant liquid component in the formulation (chloroform) and cross-checked against literature values for closely related fluoropolymers (e.g., poly(trifluoroethyl methacrylate), reported n ≈ 1.44). We have added this clarification to the manuscript as shown below:
“Volumetric 3D Printing. Volumetric 3D printing was performed using the Tomolite v2.0 (405 nm light source) from Readily 3D. In Apparite 1.2.4, the following settings were applied: “Refractive Index” set to 1.450 (chosen to match the dominant solvent, chloroform, and consistent with related fluorinated monomers such as poly(trifluoroethyl methacrylate, n ≈ 1.44)), “Absorption” set to 2.00 cm⁻¹ (base-10 absorbance A ≈ μ/ln 10 = 0.87 cm⁻¹, consistent with UV–Vis A ≈ 0.85–0.87 cm⁻¹), “Bulk Length” set to “Off,” and “Bulk Strength” set to “Off.” The test tube was measured for the vial profile, with the “Glass” type set to BK7, an “Outer Diameter” of 7.49 mm, and a “Thickness” of 0.92 mm. After volumetric printing, the print was rinsed with acetone to remove uncured resin, followed by post-curing with UV-A light (365 nm, 5 mW cm⁻², 2 h). After post-curing, the prints were air-dried.”
5. Resolution issue – feature size. The authors report feature sizes down to 15.5 µm (negative one) as the “smallest negative features reported to date for volumetric 3D printing” and highlight this fact in the abstract. How the authors can explained such resolution? Is it due to the chemistry (and why)? Or is it due to the optical system? Can they give details about the optical configuration of their printer?
According to the current experimental data, this statement is overexaggerated. The provided optical microscopic images do not allow reliable conclusions to be drawn regarding the resolution achieved. It is difficult to determine whether this is due to an actual resolution limitation, a fabrication artefact, or surface defects. It is recommended to acquire higher-quality images, particularly using a scanning electron microscope (SEM), in order to confirm the observations. CAD model should be provided to discuss printing fidelity and state on the merit of the chemistry or optical set-up. The choice of the « Klein bottle » object for evaluating resolution appears to be poorly suited. It would be preferable to use a standardized test object, such as a grid pattern or regularly spaced lines, to allow a more rigorous and objective assessment of resolution performance. More interesting/convincing will be the printing of the microfluidic chip with internal channel of 15.5 µm width and few millimetres length (see Gong et al. Lab Chip, 2017, 17, 2899, DOI: 10.1039/c7lc00644f, Custom 3D printer and resin for 18 μm × 20 μm microfluidic flow channels).
6. Printing fidelity. In a general manner, the CAD models should be provided with the expected dimension to assess the printing fidelity. For instance, in Figure 3b, the microfluidic system seems to be distorted (inhomogeneous geometry). Is this an expected phenomenon or a fabrication defect? Printing fidelity to be discussed.
Combined response to reviewer comments 5 and 6:
Thank you for the thoughtful critique of the feature-size claim and the request for clearer evidence of fidelity. We agree that the earlier abstract gave undue weight to a single minimum value relative to the evidence shown—a tendency that is common in reports on tomographic volumetric printing. In the revision, the claim is reframed: we report reproducible feature sizes with explicit CAD linkage across several demanding geometries, while keeping the central contribution—volumetric 3D printing of a fluorinated network together with closed-loop chemical recycling of the fluorinated content—front and center.
In tomographic volumetric printing, the smallest reliably formed feature is not dictated by optics alone. It reflects the design-dependent computational contrast in the back-projection, resin kinetics around gelation, viscosity with associated diffusion and sedimentation during and after exposure, polymerization shrinkage, and post-processing choices such as wash solvent and time. Because these factors couple, assigning a particular small feature to a single cause would be speculative and lies beyond the scope of the present work. Rather than advancing an ultimate resolution limit, we document what is reproducibly achieved under clearly specified conditions and provide the information needed for others to interpret those outcomes.
To position the results, the Supporting Information now includes a curated overview of reported feature sizes in tomographic volumetric printing derived from a screen of 37 studies; fourteen papers that list explicit numerical values were retained. Table S1 collates those minima to indicate what has been achieved in the field and to contextualize the condition-bound features reported here. As noted in your comment, many publications present a single “best-case” feature size without linking back to design. In tomographic volumetric 3D printing, such single-feature reporting is not adequate due to its relatively low computational contrast (i.e., the difference between the light dose that in-part and out-of-part voxels receive), as compared to stereolithography (SLA) or digital light processing (DLP), where out-of-part voxels typically don’t receive any light (i.e., perfect computational contrast). As a result, the out-of-part voxels fundamentally limit the dose that in-part voxels can receive, and, therefore, the apparent feature size can depend strongly on the washing step. In the revised manuscript, we make this linkage explicit.
We also strengthened the experimental evidence underlying our values. The single-geometry showcase has been replaced by a multi-geometry presentation. For each design, we report the measured feature size alongside the corresponding CAD dimension at that exact location, so any deviation is explicit. The images show continuous features rather than surface artefacts, addressing the fidelity concern, and the CAD files with nominal dimensions are provided so readers can assess fidelity directly. Optical microscopy is retained because the features are clearly resolved at the stated scales; SEM is not required to substantiate the widths we report.
The following text has been added to the Supporting Information:
“S3. Feature-size in tomographic volumetric 3D printing. In tomographic volumetric printing, the smallest reliably formed feature is not dictated by optics alone. It is governed by the design-dependent computational contrast in back-projection, resin kinetics around gelation, viscosity together with diffusion and sedimentation during and after exposure, polymerization shrinkage, and post-processing choices such as wash solvent and time. Rather than advancing an ultimate resolution limit, we document what is reproducibly achieved under fixed conditions and provide the information needed for others to interpret those outcomes.
S3.1 Literature positioning of volumetric 3D printing resolution. To contextualize the obtained feature sizes in the current work, we screened 37 publications on tomographic volumetric 3D printing and retained 14 that report explicit numerical values (restricted to tomographic volumetric 3D printing and excluding post-sintered ceramics). Table S1 collates these reported minima. Only two papers provide a direct design-to- measurement comparison: Kelly et al. (2019) report a 200 µm tail-fin tip radius versus a 400 µm design (sharper than intended), and Orth et al. (2023) report 195–200 µm versus ~180 µm for a gyroid wall and 580 µm versus ~500 µm for a pore. Most articles list single ‘best-case’ values with little to no linkage to CAD or reproducibility. The purpose of Table S1 is transparency: to position achievable feature sizes in tomographic volumetric printing and to provide readers with context for interpreting the condition-bound feature sizes reported here.
S3.2 Experimental and theoretical feature sizes of volumetric 3D printed constructs. Figure S8 pairs each CAD model with its simulated back-projection contrast and a micrograph at the narrowest measured element. Across the four designs shown, the smallest observed features are ~56 µm, ~66 µm, ~97 µm, and ~254 µm; the corresponding CAD dimensions at those exact locations are indicated in the contrast panels. Set against the survey in Table S1, these values sit among the smallest polymer features reported for tomographic volumetric printing. Only a few studies approach this scale with comparable clarity of reporting; notably, Toombs et al. (2022) demonstrate ~20 µm polymer features on a different platform. It should be noted that the very small ‘positive’ values reported by Bernal et al. (2022) and by Falandt et al. (2023) correspond to the outermost tip of a star-shaped element; such apex measurements are highly sensitive to washing and do not represent generally reproducible line or strut widths.
The gap between CAD and experiment is expected. In tomographic exposure, the achievable width at a given location is governed by local computational contrast from back-projection, the resin’s conversion profile near gelation, and the subsequent washing step, which can remove weakly crosslinked material at feature edges. Additional contributors include polymerization shrinkage and any swelling or surface relaxation during post-processing. Because most papers in the field report single ‘best-case’ numbers without CAD-to-measurement linkage—Kelly et al. (2019) and Orth et al. (2023) are rare exceptions—Figure S8 provides that linkage explicitly so that readers can interpret the condition-bound features observed here.

Response to the reviewer comment:
The authors agree that rigor around the recycling step is essential. Because all three reviewers independently raised this point, we executed a full condition matrix and were able to increase the recovery of the fluorinated monomer to 97.4 % ± 2.1 %. Thus, 97.4% of the fluorinated monomer is recovered after the first recycle–reuse loop, and that retained fraction compounds with each additional loop. In practice, this means that about 88% remains after five cycles and about 77% remains after ten cycles.
We systematically screened NaOH concentrations of 1.0, 2.5, and 5.0 M at 85 °C across hydrolytic degradation times ranging from 0.5 to 16 h. For each condition, we executed the complete workflow—alkaline reflux depolymerization, liquid–liquid extraction, aqueous washing/neutralization, and drying— with identical resin mass and solution volume. This investigation, initiated by the reviewers’ comments, increased the fluorinated-monomer recovery to 97.4% ± 2.1% at 2.5 M NaOH for 3 h, and is now used throughout the manuscript. Finally, repeatability at this condition was confirmed in triplicate (s.d. = 2.1%), significantly reducing cumulative loss over multiple reuse cycles.
We have included the following discussion related to the parameter screening into the main manuscript:
“After establishing a general workflow—alkaline reflux depolymerization, neutralization, purification, and drying— through which the fluorinated diol could be recovered from volumetrically 3D printed constructs, the degradation conditions were optimized to maximize the chemical recycling yield of the fluorinated diol (Section S5). More precisely, a condition screen at 85 °C was performed across NaOH concentrations of 1.0, 2.5, and 5.0 M and depolymerization times from 0.5–16 h, executing the complete sequence for every timepoint. The optimal condition (2.5 M NaOH for 3 h) afforded a recovery of 97.4 % ± 2.1 % (n = 3). At this per-cycle recovery, the theoretical retained fraction after ten recycle–reuse cycles is ≈76.8 % of the original fluorinated content (see Supporting Information, Section S5, for the full data and calculations).
The recovery–time profiles delineate two regimes, depicted in Figure S10. In the kinetic regime, yield increases to a concentration-dependent maximum that is reached earlier at higher [NaOH] (5 M: ~1–1.5 h; 2.5 M: ~3 h; 1 M: no maximum within 16 h). This trend is consistent with base-catalyzed urethane cleavage in which the apparent rate scales with hydroxide activity (pseudo-first-order, 𝑘 ≈ 𝑘 [𝑂𝐻−]). Beyond the maximum, the 𝑜𝑏𝑠 𝑏 isolated yield declines at 2.5–5 M and approaches a plateau. It is hypothesized that the gradual formation of crosslinked/aggregated side-product particulates during prolonged alkaline treatment physically entrap a fraction of the fluorinated diol and resist subsequent extraction. Once the population of such particulates saturates, the recovery approaches the observed plateau. The optimum at 2.5 M, 3 h therefore marks the intersection of fast cleavage kinetics with minimal secondary entrainment, resulting in a recycling yield of the fluorinated monomer of 97.4 % ± 2.1 % (n = 3).”

“Chemical recycling of HDF-OH from HDF-X. Prior to alkaline cleavage, volumetrically printed constructs were briefly ground with a mortar and pestle to eliminate geometry- dependent effects during degradation. A condition screen was performed at 85 °C under reflux, varying [NaOH] to 1.0, 2.5, and 5.0 M, and reaction time (0.5–16 h). For each condition, the same resin mass and solution volume were used and the full workflow was executed—alkaline depolymerization → neutralization to pH ≈ 7 with 1 M HCl → solvent removal by rotary evaporation → dissolution of the residue in diethyl ether (Et₂O) → filtration of insolubles → solvent removal → drying—to isolate HDF-OH (see Supporting Information Section S5). The optimized condition was identified as 2.5 M NaOH for 3 h at 85 °C, which afforded 97.4 % ± 2.1 % recovery (n = 3). For a representative batch, ground material (300 mg) was charged to a 50 mL round-bottom flask with 10 mL of 2.5 M NaOH and heated at 85 °C under reflux for 3 h. The reaction mixture was then neutralized to pH ≈ 7 by gradual addition of 1 M HCl. After neutralization, acetone was added to the aqueous phase (1:1 v/v water:acetone) to facilitate co-evaporation and streamline water removal during rotary evaporation. The mixture was concentrated by rotary evaporation to remove water and acetone, affording a solid residue. The residue was dissolved in diethyl ether (Et₂O), and the mixture was filtered to remove insoluble inorganic and polymeric by-products. The Et₂O-soluble fraction was collected, while the retained solids were washed thoroughly with deionized water to remove NaCl and other inorganic residues, then rinsed with hexane to displace residual water. The washed solids were subsequently re- extracted with Et₂O to recover any remaining HDF-OH. The combined Et₂O extracts were concentrated by rotary evaporation, and the resulting product was dried under vacuum at 40 °C for 2 h to afford purified HDF-OH, which was then re-functionalized as described in the preceding section.”
On the request for multiple recycle–reuse loops: our closed-loop design targets chemical recycling to the identical fluorinated monomer (HDF-OH). Given the fact that we verified chemical identity (NMR/MS) and property parity upon reprinting (thermal/mechanical metrics within statistical variation), running additional physical cycles does not probe a changing material state (unlike vitrimers or mechanical reprocessing, where properties can drift with each pass); it primarily tests process robustness. We therefore report the analytically grounded cumulative retention fₙ = rⁿ (with r measured at the optimized condition) and perform only one cycle experimentally.
Regarding geometry and diffusion limits during degradation: prior to alkaline cleavage, all printed parts were ground to a powder. As a result, the original object shape and dimensions do not govern recovery time in our protocol; kinetics are controlled by solution conditions and the extraction sequence. The following sentence is stated in the experimental part of the paper: “Prior to alkaline degradation, volumetrically printed constructs were briefly ground with a mortar and pestle to eliminate geometry-dependent effects during degradation.”
Finally, we have now specified the shapes/dimensions of the printed objects used for recycling and for mechanical testing in the Experimental section, as shown: “Bars with a length of 10 mm, a thickness of 1 mm, and a width of 4 mm, were volumetrically 3D printed and evaluated.”
